newsitem.title: GERMANY: HWWA institute cuts 1997 German growth forecast.
newsitem.headline: HWWA institute cuts 1997 German growth forecast.

text.p: Germany's HWWA policy think-tank revised down its forecast on Tuesday for German economic growth to 2-1/4 percent in 1997 from 2-1/2 percent previously.

The HWWA also said it expected the budget deficit to be 3.2 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), above the three-percent goal set by the Maastricht Treaty to qualify for European economic and monetary union (EMU).
In its latest economic bulletin, the Hamburg-based HWWA said economic growth would pick up to 2-3/4 percent next year and the budget deficit would fall to 2.5 percent of GDP.
Unemployment will remain high, however, and average 4.325 million this year, or 11.2 percent of the workforce, and 4.225 million (11 percent) in 1998, the HWWA said.
Germany's recovery is picking up, but remains narrowly supported by exports. Meanwhile, consumption, construction and investment are lagging, the report added.
Wrangling in Bonn over planned tax reforms -- which have been blocked in parliament by the opposition Social Democrats -- has also created uncertainty over the economic outlook.
"The retarding effects stemming from the paralysis of economic policy are a significant cause for the slow progress of the recovery," the HWWA said.
HWWA institute cuts 1997 German growth forecast
Recovery has failed to feed through to the jobs market, where unemployment has risen sharply in recent months due mainly to a series of one-off factors.

But the HWWA said that a spate of corporate cost-cutting sparked by the strong mark in 1995 and high pay rounds that year was starting to fade. Job creation could be helped by the weaker mark and more moderate wage settlements.
Unforeseeable risks remain over plans to create a single European currency, the institute said, although it predicted a prompt start to EMU in 1999 with a large starting group.
"With the change of government in France, uncertainty over a punctual start and the lineup of participants has again increased," the HWWA said.

The report added that, facing the conflict between creating jobs and meeting strict borrowing targets, Paris would tend to plead for a "softer" interpretation of the Maastricht budget deficit criterion. That example could be followed by others.
For Germany to score a direct hit on the budget deficit goal of 3.0 percent of GDP, further savings of seven billion marks would be needed this year.

The deficit forecast of 2.5 percent of GDP for next year assumes the Bundesbank will book an extraordinary profit from revaluing its foreign exchange reserves which will be channelled into state coffers.

The economic outlook also assumes a punctual start to EMU without any significant turbulence on foreign exchange markets. The mark is also expected to depreciate somewhat on market views that the euro currency will not be as stable as the mark has been historically.
